questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the structure of a transformer?
options: A single coil of insulated wire wound onto a hard steel core
Two coils of insulated wire, called the primary and secondary coils, wound onto or linked by a common soft iron core, with no electrical connection between them
Two coils joined by a copper wire so current can flow directly from the primary to the secondary
A primary coil and a secondary coil separated only by air, with no core at all
questions.explanation: A transformer consists of two coils of insulated wire — the primary and the secondary — wound onto or linked by a common soft iron core. There is no electrical connection between the coils; energy crosses only as changing magnetic flux carried by the core.

questions.q: When an alternating current flows through the primary coil, what appears at the terminals of the secondary coil?
options: A steady DC voltage, regardless of the input
An AC voltage at a higher frequency than the primary
An AC voltage with the same frequency as the AC voltage supplied to the primary coil
No voltage, because the coils are not electrically connected
questions.explanation: An alternating current in the primary produces a constantly changing magnetic flux that threads the secondary coil. This constantly changing flux produces an AC voltage at the secondary terminals with the same frequency as the AC supplied to the primary; only the magnitude of the voltage differs.

questions.q: Using the transformer equation \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\), which transformer steps the voltage up?
options: One where the number of secondary turns \(n_s\) is greater than the number of primary turns \(n_p\)
One where \(n_s\) is less than \(n_p\)
One where \(n_s\) equals \(n_p\)
One where the core is made of a non-magnetic material
questions.explanation: From \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\): if \(n_s\) is greater than \(n_p\), the output voltage \(V_s\) is greater than the input voltage \(V_p\) — a step-up transformer. If \(n_s\) is less than \(n_p\) it is a step-down transformer. The coil with more turns is always the higher-voltage side.

questions.q: A transformer in an electric piano reduces a 240 V AC voltage to a 12.0 V AC voltage. If the secondary coil has 30 turns, calculate the number of turns in the primary coil.
working: Sanity check: the primary has more turns than the secondary, confirming a step-down transformer (240 V down to 12 V).
questions.explanation: Rearranging the transformer equation \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\) for \(n_p\) gives 600 turns. More turns on the primary side matches the voltage stepping down.

questions.q: For the same electric-piano transformer (240 V to 12.0 V, primary 600 turns, secondary 30 turns), the piano draws a current of 500 mA. Treating the transformer as ideal, calculate the current in the primary coil.
working: Check the inverse: voltage stepped down by a factor of 20, so the current steps up by 20 (25 mA to 500 mA), exactly as conservation of energy demands.
questions.explanation: For an ideal transformer the current ratio is the inverse of the turns ratio, \(\frac{I_s}{I_p} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}\), giving \(I_p = 25\,\mathrm{mA}\). Current trades off inversely with voltage.

questions.q: For an ideal transformer, the Principle of Conservation of Energy means that:
options: The secondary power always exceeds the primary power because the voltage is stepped up
The primary power equals the secondary power, so \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) and you cannot get more energy out than you put in
The frequency of the output is doubled to conserve energy
Energy is created in the iron core and added to the output
questions.explanation: In an ideal transformer there is no power loss, so the primary power equals the secondary power: \(P_p = P_s\), i.e. \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\). You cannot get more energy out of a transformer than you put into it; stepping the voltage up forces the current to step down by the same factor.

questions.q: From memory: name the three main reasons a real transformer is not 100% efficient, and how each loss is reduced.
keyPoints: Incomplete flux linkage (flux leakage): not all flux from the primary passes through the secondary — reduced by winding the coils tightly on a closed soft iron core.
Resistive heat production: current through the copper windings dissipates power as heat — reduced by using thicker, lower-resistance wire.
Eddy currents in the iron core: the changing flux induces circulating currents in the conducting core — reduced by laminating the core or using ferrites.
questions.explanation: The textbook lists exactly three causes of less-than-ideal behaviour: incomplete flux linkage, resistive heat production, and eddy currents in the iron core (the episode's hook is FRET). If you recalled all three with the correct fix on each, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: How are energy losses due to eddy currents in the iron core of a transformer reduced?
options: By using thicker copper wire for the windings
By constructing the core from many layers of iron coated with an insulator (a laminated iron core), or by using ferrites that transmit flux well but conduct electricity poorly
By winding the primary and secondary coils further apart
By running the transformer on DC instead of AC
questions.explanation: A laminated iron core — many thin iron layers separated by insulation — breaks up the eddy-current loops, greatly reducing their size and the heating losses. Ferrites are an alternative: they are good transmitters of magnetic flux but poor conductors of electricity, so eddy currents are significantly reduced. Thicker wire fixes resistive heating, not eddy currents.

questions.q: From memory, give the full causal chain for why a transformer requires an AC input and does nothing on steady DC.
keyPoints: Faraday's law: the induced EMF depends on the rate of change of flux, not the flux itself (EMF = N x change in flux / change in time).
Steady DC produces a constant flux, so the rate of change is zero, so no EMF is induced in the secondary — no sustained output (only a brief pulse at switch-on and switch-off).
AC continually reverses, producing a continuously changing flux, so the rate of change is non-zero and a continuous alternating EMF is induced.
questions.explanation: The marks live in the explicit 'no change, no EMF' step for the DC case: constant flux gives a rate of change of zero, which gives no induced EMF, which gives no output. Only AC supplies the continuously changing flux Faraday's law needs.

questions.q: A steady DC current is connected to the primary of a transformer and left on. What is the secondary output?
options: A continuous DC voltage equal to the turns ratio times the input
A continuous AC voltage at 50 Hz
No sustained output — only a single brief pulse at the instant the DC is switched on and another at switch-off
A steadily increasing voltage as flux builds up
questions.explanation: Steady DC gives a constant flux, so the rate of change of flux is zero and no EMF is induced — no sustained output. Only at switch-on (flux rising from zero) and switch-off (flux falling to zero) is the flux briefly changing, giving a single momentary pulse each time. Say 'no sustained output', not 'literally zero ever'.
